comparison: Both evaluate the core methodological claims (C2, C5, C35-C37). OpenEval finds the method SUPPORTED with converging evidence from theoretical framework and experimental validation. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, acknowledging it is 'novel and potentially powerful' but expressing 'significant concerns about several untested assumptions' and questioning whether conductance deconvolution 'may not be possible' without voltage-clamp data at multiple command voltages.

Both address linearity assumptions (C12-C14). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED, stating linearity is demonstrated experimentally and the hyperpolarization protocol minimizes voltage-dependent currents. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the I-V linearity evidence is 'helpful' but questioning whether linearity holds for synaptic conductances themselves, noting 'open rectification will be a feature of any conductance generated by asymmetric distributions of ions.'

Both evaluate conductance characterization across neuron types (C16-C26). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with comprehensive data, substantial sample sizes, and internal consistency. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, not directly critiquing the patterns but raising fundamental concerns that the in situ preparation lacks descending control and ascending feedback, which 'does need to be considered when using an approach of this type to speculate on the prevalence of specific circuit motifs.'

Both address functional interpretations and network architecture (C33-C34). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED but notes support is 'strong but indirect, relying on correlation.' Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, specifically cautioning that preparation limitations 'need to be considered when using an approach of this type to speculate on the prevalence of specific circuit motifs within the medulla.'

Both discuss methodological robustness and validation (C27, C29). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED through direct comparison of protocols and temporal stability. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, expressing concern that previous approaches used voltage-clamp at various command voltages whereas this method attempts extraction without such data, stating 'I am concerned that this simply may not be possible.'

Both evaluate reversal potential variability and timing reliability (C28-C32). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting profile shape robustness and theoretical justification from prior literature. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, not challenging these findings about reversal potential variability or timing estimate reliability.

Both address linear upper boundaries and theoretical decomposition (C49-C50). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as both methodological validation and biological finding. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, not directly addressing these claims but expressing fundamental concerns about the linear I-V assumption and conductance deconvolution that undermine confidence in theoretical interpretations.

Both evaluate the limitation acknowledgment of the reduced preparation (C52). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as an appropriate caveat. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, explicitly stating this limitation should be discussed and noting the absence of descending control and ascending feedback.

Both evaluate methodological details and quality control (C38-C39, C43-C45). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as straightforward procedural descriptions. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED, with the editor noting 'the electrophysiological techniques and results are of high quality' and acknowledging the approach is 'described well.'
OpenEval finds biological context claims (C6-C7, C15, C41-C42) SUPPORTED by extensive prior literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval finds the general statement about rhythmic circuits (C1) SUPPORTED as background context from established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
